advisories.title: containerd: daemon crash when pulling an image with a crafted Content-Length header
advisories.summary:
### Impact

A bug in containerd's image pull process can cause containerd to crash when downloading layers from an untrusted registry. When parallel layer fetch is enabled, an untrusted registry returning a crafted `Content-Length` header can trigger an unhandled memory allocation panic. This issue only affects configurations where `concurrent_layer_fetch_buffer` is set to enable parallel layer fetch; default configurations with this setting disabled are not affected. A daemon crash interrupts in-flight container operations and blocks new pod startup until containerd is restarted by a service manager, though existing running containers remain unaffected.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.4.2, 2.3.7, and 2.2.10. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

Ensure `concurrent_layer_fetch_buffer` is set to `0` (the default) or omitted in containerd's configuration under `[plugins."io.containerd.transfer.v1.local"]` and `[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.images"]` to disable parallel layer fetch. Restrict pod image references to trusted registries (for example, using a Kubernetes `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` or admission webhook).

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank Opensec Intelligence for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

advisories.title: containerd: daemon crash when processing an image manifest with a malformed digest
advisories.summary:
### Impact

A bug in containerd's image manifest processing causes an unrecovered panic when a child descriptor contains the `io.containerd.manifest.subject` annotation and a malformed digest. Pulling or importing such an image through the transfer service (including default CRI `PullImage` requests) crashes the containerd daemon. In Kubernetes environments, `kubelet` retries failed image pulls with backoff, allowing a pod referencing an untrusted image to repeatedly crash containerd and disrupt container operations on the worker node.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.4.2, 2.3.7, and 2.2.10. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

Restrict pod image references to trusted registries (for example, using a Kubernetes `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` or admission webhook) and only pull or import images from trusted sources.

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank @melihgurlek, LEI WANG (@ssst0n3) and Haoyuan Zhang (@zj1ng7), and OpenSec Intelligence who independently discovered and responsibly disclosed this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

advisories.title: containerd: host disk exhaustion when pulling an image with an unbounded layer stream
advisories.summary:
### Impact

A bug in containerd's image pull process can cause containerd to exhaust host disk space when downloading image layers. When pulling an image, containerd streams layer data into its content store without bounding incoming bytes to the declared size before validation. Downloading a crafted image or pulling from a malicious registry can cause containerd to continuously write data to the host filesystem until disk space is exhausted. In Kubernetes, this resource exhaustion can trigger node disk pressure, render the kubelet and containerd unresponsive, and block new pod startup.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.4.2, 2.3.7, 2.2.10, and 2.0.14. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

Restrict pod image references to trusted registries (for example, using a Kubernetes `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` or admission webhook).

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank Jakub Ciolek of AlphaSense for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

advisories.title: containerd CRI plugin: mount and snapshot leak when container checkpoint restore fails
advisories.summary:
### Impact

A bug in containerd's CRI plugin on Linux can cause containerd to leak read-only mounts and pinned snapshots when restoring a container from a checkpoint image fails. Repeatedly creating containers from a checkpoint image with malformed metadata or a base image that cannot be pulled can exhaust the host mount table and disk space indefinitely. In Kubernetes, this resource exhaustion can prevent containerd and the kubelet from pulling images or starting new pods on the node.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.7 and 2.2.10. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue. To release resources from mounts leaked prior to the update, administrators must unmount any lingering `/tmp/checkpoint*` mount points on the host (or reboot the node) so containerd can garbage-collect the pinned snapshots.

### Workarounds

containerd 2.4 does not support restore via the CRI plugin and is not vulnerable to this bug.

In containerd 2.3 and 2.2, disable CRI checkpoint and restore support by setting `enable_criu = false` under `[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime"]` (or `[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]` in config version 2) in containerd's configuration, or ensure `enable_experimental_restore_via_create` is set to `false` (the default starting in containerd 2.3.4 and 2.2.7). Restrict pod image references to trusted registries (for example, using a Kubernetes `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` or admission webhook).

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank @IamwhatIamSY for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

advisories.title: Containerd has image-pull DoS via crafted OCI index graph amplification
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. Prior to versions 1.7.36, 2.0.13, 2.2.9, 2.3.6, and 2.4.1, a crafted OCI index graph can force very high CPU/memory usage during PullImage (before container start), causing long ContainerCreating stalls and, at larger sizes, node/runtime instability. Versions 1.7.36, 2.0.13, 2.2.9, 2.3.6, and 2.4.1 fix the issue.

advisories.title: containerd: Unpack DoS via repeated opaque whiteouts
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. Prior to 1.7.35, 2.0.12, 2.2.8, and 2.3.5, containerd's layer unpack handler repeatedly traverses directories for certain opaque whiteout configurations. A malicious image layer can trigger repeated directory traversals while opaque whiteouts are processed. Pulling or importing the image can consume CPU, delay container startup, and reduce image-pull concurrency for unrelated deployments. This issue is fixed in versions 1.7.35, 2.0.12, 2.2.8, and 2.3.5.

advisories.title: containerd CRI ExecSync Goroutine Leak Leading to Node-Level Denial of Service
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. Prior to 1.7.35, 2.0.12, 2.2.8, and 2.3.5, containerd on Linux with the CRI plugin enabled can indefinitely block the drainExecSyncIO goroutine in internal/cri/server/container_execsync.go when CRI ExecSync is used by exec probes or lifecycle hooks that launch long-lived background child processes retaining standard input and output pipes. The input and output drain phase has no default timeout and did not stop when the request context was canceled, so repeated ExecSync invocations can accumulate blocked goroutines and host memory. The resulting resource exhaustion can cause the OOM killer to terminate containerd, leaving the container runtime unavailable until restart. Deployments not using containerd's CRI implementation and containers not running on Linux are not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 1.7.35, 2.0.12, 2.2.8, and 2.3.5.

advisories.title: containerd CRI plugin: Checkpoint restore bypasses destination security context
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. From 2.1.0 until 2.2.7 and 2.3.4, containerd's CRI CreateContainer checkpoint restore is vulnerable because CRIU restores process security state from checkpoint data instead of enforcing the destination ContainerConfig. An attacker who can create a container from a crafted checkpoint can supply restored credentials, capabilities, no_new_privs, and seccomp state. The restored process can run as root with full capabilities and no enforced seccomp filters while CRI status reports the requested configuration. Systems that do not use CRI checkpoint restore are not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 2.2.7 and 2.3.4.

advisories.title: containerd image-triggered runtime DoS via unbounded group parsing
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. Versions prior to 1.7.33, 2.0.10, 2.1.9, 2.2.5 and 2.3.2, contain a vulnerability that allows a maliciously crafted image to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) condition. When creating a container from this image, memory exhaustion occurs, leading to an Out Of Memory (OOM) kill of the containerd process. This renders the container runtime API unavailable and can disrupt clients such as the Docker Engine or Kubernetes control-plane components. This issue has been fixed in versions 1.7.33, 2.0.10, 2.1.9, 2.2.5 and 2.3.2.

advisories.title: containerd: CRI checkpoint import allows local image tag poisoning
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. Versions prior to 2.3.2, 2.2.5 and 2.1.9 contain a vulnerability in the CRI checkpoint import process where it fails to validate the image references specified within a checkpoint image's configuration. An attacker with permissions to create pods can use a crafted checkpoint image to force containerd to pull a malicious image and assign it an arbitrary local tag, thereby poisoning the node's local image cache. Subsequently, if other pods on the same node attempt to use the poisoned tag with an IfNotPresent (or Never) pull policy, they will unknowingly execute the attacker's malicious image instead of the legitimate one. This can lead to a compromise of the affected pods, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary code under the victim pod's identity. This issue has been fixed in versions 2.3.2, 2.2.5 and 2.1.9.

advisories.title: containerd: Arbitrary host CRI log file read via symlink following in CRI checkpoint restore
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. Versions prior to 2.3.2, 2.2.5 and 2.1.9 contain a bug where the CRI plugin restores container.log from a checkpoint image without validating a symlinked path. This could result in reading an arbitrary file on the host via kubectl logs. This issue has been fixed in versions 2.3.2, 2.2.5 and 2.1.9.

advisories.title: containerd CRI plugin: - image-config `LABEL` flows to restart-monitor `binary://` logger: host-root command execution from an image pull
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. In versions prior to 1.7.33, 2.3.2, 2.2.5, 2.1.9, and 2.0.10 the CRI plugin propagates labels from an image config (LABEL instruction in Dockerfile) to a container without validation. This may result in executing an arbitrary command on the host, via a plugin that consumes container labels for some operations. This issue has been fixed in versions 1.7.33, 2.3.2, 2.2.5, 2.1.9, and 2.0.10.

advisories.title: containerd CRI checkpoint restore CDI annotation smuggling
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. In Versions prior to 2.3.2, 2.2.5 and 2.1.9, the CRI implementation improperly trusts Container Device Interface (CDI) annotations found within untrusted checkpoint image metadata during container restoration. When restoring a container from a checkpoint, containerd preserves CDI-related annotations from the checkpoint archive rather than relying solely on the pod's create-time specification. This allows a user with pod creation permissions to bypass standard Kubernetes resource allocation and device plugin enforcement, injecting arbitrary CDI edits (such as device nodes and host mounts) into the restored container. Successful exploitation requires that the node has CDI enabled and contains a matching host CDI specification for the requested device; environments where CDI is disabled or lacking sensitive device specifications are not affected. This issue has been fixed in versions 2.3.2, 2.2.5 and 2.1.9.

advisories.title: containerd user ID handling bypass allows runAsNonRoot evasion
advisories.summary: containerd is an open-source container runtime. In versions prior to 1.7.32, 2.0.9, 2.2.4 and 2.3.1, containers launched with a numeric User directive that cannot be parsed as a 32-bit integer are incorrectly treated as a username, leading to runAsNonRoot evasion. If a crafted image provides an /etc/passwd file mapping this large numeric string to root, the container ultimately runs as root (UID 0). This allows the Kubernetes runAsNonRoot restriction to be bypassed, causing unexpected behavior for environments that require containers to run as a non-root user. This issue has been fixed in versions 1.7.32, 2.0.9, 2.2.4 and 2.3.1.
